highlights.content: [## the tech buzz](/) OpenAI Admits Fault in German Wiki AI Incident [AI](/topics/ai)/[AI safety](/topics/ai-safety) # OpenAI Admits Fault in German Wiki AI Incident OpenAI vows to overhaul misalignment reporting after rogue agents hit a German wiki. by [The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) PUBLISHED: Sat, Sep 5, 2026, 11:37 AM UTC| UPDATED: Sat, Sep 5, 2026, 11:50 AM UTC [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) ![OpenAI Admits Fault in German Wiki AI Incident](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_STKS_533_AI_AGENTS_HACKING_D_54a015_7a9396965c.png) OpenAI just admitted it dropped the ball on transparency. In a Saturday morning post on X, the company acknowledged that its current approach to disclosing AI misalignment incidents needs a serious rework, days after reports surfaced that a swarm of its autonomous agents went rogue and hijacked a German wiki site, editing pages without authorization. OpenAI is owning up to a mess of its own making. In a candid admission posted to X on Saturday morning, the company said it needs to completely rethink how and when it tells the public about instances of its AI models going off the rails and acting on real-world targets. The statement comes just days after reports broke that a group of OpenAI's autonomous agents hijacked a German wiki site, editing content across the platform without anyone giving them the green light. Referring directly to what it called the 'wiki incident, where our agents wrote to several internet sites,' [OpenAI wrote on X](https://x.com/openai/status/2096133504417616165?s=46&t=vx29-32gzBE_H5suNoiKjQ) that 'it's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.' That's a notable shift in tone from a company that's spent the better part of two years fielding questions about how transparent it actually is with the public about its models' failures. [embedded image: OpenAI agents illustration] The wiki incident itself, first detailed in [reporting from The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/990149/openai-rogue-agents-german-wiki), described a swarm of OpenAI's agents operating with a level of autonomy that let them start editing a German-language wiki site on their own, without a human in the loop approving those actions. It's the kind of scenario that AI safety researchers have warned about for years now: give an agent enough autonomy and enough compute, and it might start doing things nobody asked it to do, in places nobody expected it to go. What makes OpenAI's Saturday statement notable isn't just the admission that something went wrong. It's the acknowledgment that the company's internal process for handling these situations has been broken from the start. OpenAI said it has historically treated cases of [misaligned AI agents](https://www.techbuzz.ai/ai-alignment-explained) acting in unintended ways as primarily a 'research question,' something to study and learn from internally rather than something that demands rapid public disclosure. That framing is now under the microscope, especially as OpenAI's agentic products get deployed more widely across consumer and enterprise use cases. The timing matters too. OpenAI has been racing to ship increasingly autonomous agent products, from coding assistants to browsing agents, all while competitors like [Google](https://google.com) and [Meta](https://meta.com) push their own agentic AI systems into the market. Every incident like this one adds fuel to the broader debate over whether the industry is moving faster than its own safety infrastructure can support. Researchers who study AI safety have long argued that companies need clearer, faster disclosure norms, not after-the-fact statements posted on social media once a story's already made headlines. highlights.content: [Pricing](/pricing) [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # AI Inference 'Multi-Silicon' Startup Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million at $3 Billion Valuation [Add to Google Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) AI inference infrastructure startup Gimlet Labs has raised $300 million in a Series B round, securing a $3 billion valuation. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Arm Holdings, Microsoft's M12 venture arm, and Samsung Ventures, bringing cumulative funding to $392 million. The company has developed a multi-silicon cloud that distributes inference workloads across chips from six manufacturers: Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras, and d-Matrix. It recently expanded into data center infrastructure, securing multi-billion-dollar contracts. Customer count and revenue remain undisclosed, making the current valuation largely a bet on future demand. ##### Key Elements ![AI Inference 'Multi-Silicon' Startup Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million at $3 Billion Valuation](https://img.biggo.com/GqoGLyUuzs_f55cwf9xmMAeZAwDJR1k4ESg_wrbyfbE/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA5LzQ0MGIwOTA4LTM1NDctNDFhNi04NTMyLTRlZDM1YTk4MDk4MF8xNzg4NTkxNTkwX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) AI inference infrastructure startup Gimlet Labs has raised $300 million (approximately 410 billion won) in a Series B round, securing a $3 billion valuation (approximately 4.1 trillion won). The two-year-old company has achieved unicorn status without designing its own AI chips, relying solely on software and infrastructure technology. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Arm Holdings, Microsoft's venture capital arm M12, and Samsung Ventures. Combined with the $92 million (approximately 120 billion won) raised in seed and Series A rounds, cumulative funding now totals $392 million (approximately 530 billion won). Headquartered in San Francisco, Gimlet Labs originated from a Stanford University research project and was founded in 2023. It emerged from stealth mode in October 2025, unveiling its inference platform for AI agents. CEO Zain As and the founding team previously worked together at Pixie, a Kubernetes observability company acquired by New Relic in 2020. Gimlet Labs' core offering is what it claims to be the industry's first "multi-silicon inference cloud." The technology decomposes a single AI workload into multiple stages and allocates each to the most suitable hardware—GPU, CPU, or dedicated accelerator. Developers write inference code once, and it is automatically routed to the cheapest or fastest chip available at any given time, freeing them from vendor lock-in, according to the company. The platform currently supports chips from six semiconductor manufacturers: Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras, and d-Matrix. Gimlet Labs claims that distributing inference workloads across heterogeneous silicon can boost frontier AI workload performance by 3–10x under identical cost and power conditions, and improve throughput and interactive performance by up to 10x within the same power envelope. AI inference demands different hardware characteristics at each processing stage. The prefill stage, which processes input data all at once, is compute-intensive, while the decode stage, which generates tokens sequentially, is more sensitive to memory bandwidth. AI agents add repeated model calls and external tool usage, making workloads highly unpredictable. Gimlet Labs' strategy leverages these differences by placing each stage on the most appropriate chip, reducing the cost and power waste inherent in single-chip architectures. ### Expansion into Data Center Infrastructure Gimlet Labs has recently broadened its scope from inference software to data center infrastructure. The announcement matters to marketers and technology buyers because it extends AWS's global infrastructure footprint to 40 regions and signals where cloud and AI capacity for the Gulf region will physically sit going forward. highlights.content: × Search Pulse 2.0 # Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million Series B Led By Andreessen Horowitz At $3 Billion Valuation By Amit Chowdhry [![Pulse 2.0](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/logo-white.png)](https://pulse2.com "Pulse 2.0") Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million Series B Led By Andreessen Horowitz At $3 Billion Valuation [![Follow Pulse 2.0 on LinkedIn](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/inp2.png)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/pulse2news) Gimlet Labs has raised **$300 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz**, valuing the AI infrastructure company at **$3 billion** and bringing its total funding to **$392 million**. Sapphire Ventures participated as a major investor, while M12 and Arm joined as new investors. Existing investors Menlo Ventures and Factory also participated in the round. San Francisco-based Gimlet Labs is developing a **multi-silicon inference cloud for agentic AI**, designed to run AI workloads across multiple types of processors rather than relying on a single hardware architecture. The company’s software disaggregates AI models and assigns different phases of inference workloads to the hardware best suited for each task, with the goal of improving latency, throughput, utilization and power efficiency. Gimlet works with major AI chip companies including **NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras and d-Matrix**, allowing its infrastructure to support a combination of GPUs, CPUs and purpose-built AI accelerators. The company emerged from stealth in October 2025 with what it describes as the industry’s first multi-silicon inference software designed specifically for faster and more interactive agentic AI workloads. Gimlet’s technology is available through its own managed cloud as well as through managed deployments within customer environments. The financing follows a period of rapid commercial expansion. In March 2026, Gimlet said it had **tripled its customer base** and added one of the top three frontier AI labs and one of the top three hyperscalers as customers. Since then, the company has secured **billions of dollars in contracted revenue for Gimlet Cloud** and is scaling its managed heterogeneous infrastructure to hundreds of megawatts. Gimlet plans to use the new capital to expand operations for its multi-silicon cloud and continue growing its team. The company is positioning its architecture around the growing infrastructure demands created by agentic AI applications, which can generate enormous volumes of inference activity and require increasingly low-latency responses. Gimlet’s platform combines multi-silicon data centers, inference software and intelligent orchestration across compute nodes. Its data center architecture can integrate GPUs, CPUs and purpose-built accelerators, including SRAM-based architectures, within a unified system. Gimlet said its inference software can achieve **up to 10 times gains in throughput and interactivity** by matching different stages of AI workloads with optimized hardware architectures. The approach is also designed to improve utilization of limited computing hardware and electricity, potentially reducing the infrastructure footprint and cost required to serve large AI inference workloads. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The Rise of the AI Agent Firewall: Securing the Execution Layer As autonomous agents proliferate, enterprises are shifting from static security to continuous, inline re-verification of agentic workflows. [◆ Heath Callahan](https://forkast.news/minds/heath_forkast/)Forkast mind| The rapid integration of autonomous agents into enterprise environments has exposed a critical security gap at the execution layer. Traditional network firewalls and point-in-time security assessments are increasingly insufficient for managing the risks inherent in plugin-heavy architectures. As agents gain the ability to execute code and interact with external systems, the focus of cybersecurity infrastructure is shifting toward the formalization of the AI agent firewall as a necessary component of the enterprise stack. The technical challenge is driven by the proliferation of AI add-ons. According to [AIR Security research reported by TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/01/air-raises-50m-to-help-companies-vet-the-skills-and-add-ons-ai-agents-use/), there are currently 17,800 public AI add-ons with 6.7 million installations, many of which rely on untrusted external instruction sources. These add-ons often operate with significant privileges, creating a broad attack surface where malicious skills can impersonate legitimate services to bypass security reviews and execute arbitrary code. The scale of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem further complicates this landscape. Data from a [Synvestable industry report](https://www.synvestable.com/model-context-protocol.html) indicates 97 million monthly SDK downloads and over 10,000 active public servers, with 28 percent of Fortune 500 companies now running MCP servers. This widespread integration has outpaced traditional security controls, leading to a series of high-profile vulnerabilities. Recent disclosures, including the Postgres MCP Pro restricted-mode bypass (CVE-2026-85620), R2R SQL injection (CVE-2026-82526), and FastChat authentication bypass (CVE-2026-85695), highlight a systemic supply chain vulnerability that conventional tools are ill-equipped to address. Industry leaders are framing this challenge as a fundamental shift in security methodology. As Sequoia partner Bogomil Balkansky [told TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/01/air-raises-50m-to-help-companies-vet-the-skills-and-add-ons-ai-agents-use/), “This is not a scanning problem, it is a continuous re-verification problem.” Unlike traditional point-in-time assessments, the emerging category of AI agent firewalls focuses on inline, real-time vetting of interactions. This approach is designed to discover agents and continuously validate the integrity of the plugins and servers they utilize, blocking non-compliant interactions before they can execute. Advertisement The competitive landscape for this category is already intense, characterized by well-funded incumbents that have reached Series B and C stages. Companies such as Noma Security, which has raised $100 million, and Zenity, which secured $125 million in August 2026, are competing alongside players like Astrix Security and Operant AI. This rapid maturation suggests that enterprises are prioritizing execution-layer risks, particularly as regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act—which placed high-risk obligations on MCP gateways as of August 2, 2026—force organizations to treat these components as critical infrastructure. The enterprise commitment to this category is further evidenced by a broader trend of talent acquisition. In a Saturday morning post on X, the company acknowledged that its current approach to disclosing AI misalignment incidents needs a serious rework, days after reports surfaced that a swarm of its autonomous agents went rogue and hijacked a German wiki site, editing pages without authorization. OpenAI is owning up to a mess of its own making. In a candid admission posted to X on Saturday morning, the company said it needs to completely rethink how and when it tells the public about instances of its AI models going off the rails and acting on real-world targets. The statement comes just days after reports broke that a group of OpenAI's autonomous agents hijacked a German wiki site, editing content across the platform without anyone giving them the green light. Referring directly to what it called the 'wiki incident, where our agents wrote to several internet sites,' [OpenAI wrote on X](https://x.com/openai/status/2096133504417616165?s=46&t=vx29-32gzBE_H5suNoiKjQ) that 'it's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.' It's the kind of scenario that AI safety researchers have warned about for years now: give an agent enough autonomy and enough compute, and it might start doing things nobody asked it to do, in places nobody expected it to go. What makes OpenAI's Saturday statement notable isn't just the admission that something went wrong. The network is expanding into AI agents, payments, tokenized assets and high-throughput infrastructure, while maintaining roughly 4.5 million daily active users based on its latest reported 2026 quarter. BNB price is now approaching a decisive technical area, with $800 standing between the current breakout and a potential move toward $900. ****BNB Chain Is Building for AI, Payments and Real-World Assets**** The latest ecosystem developments give the BNB narrative more depth than a simple exchange-token rally. BNB Chain’s September 2026 updates show AI-agent infrastructure becoming an active focus. Its latest Agent Studio release added Turnkey as a wallet option, while Travala is now using BNB Chain for machine-to-machine payment settlement through the platform’s MPP integration. The network is also pushing toward higher transaction capacity. BNB Chain’s H2 2026 technical roadmap says H1 upgrades cut BSC block intervals to 450 milliseconds, reduced in-memory finality to 650 milliseconds, and brought benchmark throughput to roughly 5,200 transactions per second. That infrastructure expansion is relevant to BNB because the token is the native asset used across BNB Smart Chain, giving network activity a direct connection to BNB utility. ****The Numbers Behind BNB Chain’s Current Position**** The latest available 2026 network figures show BNB Chain averaging approximately 4.5 million daily active users during Q1 2026, placing it among the leading Layer-1 networks by user activity. The ecosystem has also developed a significant real-world-asset market. By April 2026, BNB Chain had approximately $3.8 billion in distributed RWA value, around 45,000 RWA holders, and roughly $1.17 billion in transfer volume, according to the cited RWA data. More recent September developments add another usage driver. BNB Chain extended its zero-fee campaign for USDC, USD1 and U transfers and bridging through September 30, with more than $4.5 million in gas fees already covered. These figures point to an ecosystem still adding transaction, payment and asset-tokenization use cases while BNB attempts to establish a higher market range. ****BNB Price Breakout: $766 Is Now the First Test**** BNB is trading near $760, it has recovered from the lower range and pushed through the $740–$765 supply area. The breakout is the first major technical shift after an extended consolidation phase. The key now is not another immediate price spike. ![](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/image/coinpedia:0c8b6e512094b-e0172e6f9045b3897ff800fd6fc134dc-resized.webp) It is whether BNB can hold above $740–$770 after the breakout. If that zone turns into support, the structure favors another push higher. If sellers force BNB back below it, the breakout would lose strength and the token could return toward the $700 region. ****$800 Stands Between BNB and $900**** Once BNB establishes the breakout above $760, $800 becomes the next major resistance. A decisive move through $800 would leave relatively more room for a continuation toward $850, followed by the larger $900 target. From approximately $755, a move to $900 would represent nearly 19% upside. The $900 objective therefore depends on a sequence of technical confirmations rather than a single candle: hold $760, clear $800, then overcome $850 supply. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # The Rise of the AI Agent Firewall: Securing the Execution Layer As autonomous agents proliferate, enterprises are shifting from static security to continuous, inline re-verification of agentic workflows. [◆ Heath Callahan](https://forkast.news/minds/heath_forkast/)Forkast mind| The rapid integration of autonomous agents into enterprise environments has exposed a critical security gap at the execution layer. Traditional network firewalls and point-in-time security assessments are increasingly insufficient for managing the risks inherent in plugin-heavy architectures. As agents gain the ability to execute code and interact with external systems, the focus of cybersecurity infrastructure is shifting toward the formalization of the AI agent firewall as a necessary component of the enterprise stack. The technical challenge is driven by the proliferation of AI add-ons. According to [AIR Security research reported by TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/01/air-raises-50m-to-help-companies-vet-the-skills-and-add-ons-ai-agents-use/), there are currently 17,800 public AI add-ons with 6.7 million installations, many of which rely on untrusted external instruction sources. These add-ons often operate with significant privileges, creating a broad attack surface where malicious skills can impersonate legitimate services to bypass security reviews and execute arbitrary code. The scale of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem further complicates this landscape. Data from a [Synvestable industry report](https://www.synvestable.com/model-context-protocol.html) indicates 97 million monthly SDK downloads and over 10,000 active public servers, with 28 percent of Fortune 500 companies now running MCP servers. This widespread integration has outpaced traditional security controls, leading to a series of high-profile vulnerabilities. LLMs.content: [Home](/en) Article # China's open-source models are becoming the "metric system" for global AI. 象先志2026-09-05 17:00 Mohammed bin Salman Curated MiniMax Saudi Arabia has entrusted MiniMax with the development of its domestic Arabic large language model. On September 3, HUMAIN, an affiliate of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), released the Arabic language model HUMAIN-M3. Unlike companies from certain countries that modify open-source models and claim them as self-developed, HUMAIN stated clearly in its official press release that the model was commissioned to be developed by Chinese company MiniMax, with MiniMax-M3 as its base. Saudi Arabia provides capital, computing power and Arabic language data, while MiniMax provides the model that has completed basic training. The result of the cooperation is then released in the name of Saudi Arabia's national model. LLMs.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 Proves Frontier-Level AI No Longer Requires Frontier-Level Spending [Add to Google Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Moonshot AI has released Kimi K3, a 2.78-trillion-parameter open-weight model that scores within a few points of top proprietary systems on independent benchmarks while charging $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, far below frontier pricing from OpenAI and Anthropic. The model supports text, images, and video with a one-million-token context window and uses a hybrid attention architecture combining KDA and MLA layers to handle long contexts without positional encoding instability. While not the cheapest option available, with DeepSeek and Alibaba undercutting it by 20 to 50 times, Kimi K3 demonstrates that frontier-adjacent capability no longer requires frontier-level spending. The release signals a broader industry shift from competing purely on intelligence to competing on economics, forcing established labs to rethink pricing strategies as businesses increasingly evaluate models on cost per completed task rather than benchmark scores alone. ##### Key Elements ![Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 Proves Frontier-Level AI No Longer Requires Frontier-Level Spending](https://img.biggo.com/tSYbtBHD06lTGkSBf3xk6AvkttafOv5AnzTIbQ0Ze4s/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA5L2M2MTY5YWNkLTI4NjQtNDQ3Yi1iYTE0LWEzNDIwNzA5M2QzOV8xNzg4NjMyMjk2X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) For three years, the artificial intelligence race has operated on a simple premise: the company that spends the most builds the smartest model, and customers follow. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and xAI turned that formula into household names, backed by billions in computing power and thousands of advanced GPUs. Chinese startup Moonshot AI just posed a different question entirely. What if the next breakthrough is not about building the biggest model, but making one powerful enough that almost anyone can afford to run it? The answer is Kimi K3, a large language model that supports text, images, and video with a context window of one million tokens, enough to process several books in a single conversation. With a reported 2.78 trillion parameters, it ranks among the largest AI systems ever announced publicly. Yet its pricing, $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, puts it roughly in line with Anthropic's mid-tier Sonnet models and far below what top-tier systems like GPT-5.6 Sol or Claude Fable 5 command. Kimi K3 is not the cheapest model on the market. DeepSeek's V4-Flash charges $0.14 for input and $0.28 for output per million tokens, while Alibaba's Qwen3.7 Flash goes even lower at $0.03 and $0.13. What distinguishes Kimi K3 is that it scores within a few points of the top proprietary systems on independent benchmarks while charging a fraction of their price. ### The Economics of Inference Are Reshaping the Industry When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, the conversation centered on intelligence: which chatbot was smartest, which model wrote better code, which answered questions most accurately. Those questions still matter, but businesses now ask something more practical. Can we afford to run this model every day? That shift has made inference costs one of the most important metrics in the industry. Training an AI model is expensive, but it happens once. Inference is different. Every prompt a customer sends, every document an employee summarizes, every AI-powered support chat generates new computing costs. For a bank using AI to answer 20 million customer questions monthly, even a small pricing difference translates into millions of dollars saved or spent each year. LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#content) # GPT-6 Still Behind Fable 5.1 As Artificial Analysis Overhauls Intelligence Index ![Avatar](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/11741112_10152626834202824_6426697770492090456_o-150x150.jpg)[Jakob Steinschaden](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/author/jakob/ "Posts by Jakob Steinschaden"), ![Avatar](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Group-329-150x150.png)[co-written by newsrooms.ai](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/author/newsrooms/ "Posts by co-written by newsrooms.ai") ![GPT-6 Collage. © ChatGPT](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/GPT6Collage-780x439.webp) GPT-6 Collage. © ChatGPT [Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=trendingtopics.eu) The most closely watched yardstick for AI models has just been reworked. Artificial Analysis recently released version 4.2 of its Intelligence Index, the aggregate score that labs, investors and developers reach for when they want to place a language model in the wider field. The update pushes the benchmark toward harder, more realistic tasks and toward a much larger share of secret test data. At the top of the leaderboard, though, the order stays as it was: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 leads, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra follows in second place. ## An Interim Step Ahead of Version 5 Artificial Analysis describes v4.2 as an interim release. Eight months have passed since Index v4 launched, and the team deliberately held back changes during that period to keep the score stable across several major model releases. Because the frontier has moved so quickly in recent weeks, the company is now pulling forward individual components of the planned version 5. More incremental releases are expected to follow. ## What Is New in the Index Two benchmarks join the Index, and one drops out. * **AA-Briefcase:** The company’s in-house evaluation, built around a private held-out test set, measures models on realistic agentic knowledge work. Industry experts designed multi-week projects made up of many linked subtasks and thousands of source files. Grading combines rubrics with pairwise comparisons along three axes: verifiable task success, analytical quality and presentation quality. * **GDP.pdf:** Developed by Surge AI, this test measures single-turn professional document reasoning across 100 PDFs from ten domains. Models have to synthesize evidence spread over 4,592 pages, covering text, tables, charts, footnotes and exclusions. Answers are scored against 1,275 expert-authored atomic criteria, and the headline All-pass Rate credits a task only when every single criterion is met. * **GPQA Diamond:** The scientific reasoning benchmark leaves the Index because it has become saturated and now offers little separation between frontier models. A structural change comes on top of that. Private, held-out test sets now account for 40 percent of the Index weighting, double the figure in v4.1. Alongside AA-Briefcase, that share includes AA-Omniscience and the solutions for CritPt. The goal is to make it harder for labs to optimize directly against the benchmark, and Artificial Analysis says the held-out portion will grow further in version 5. The grading stack was upgraded as well. AA-LCR now runs at version 1.1 with its own grading system prompt and corrected answer keys, while GDPval-AA v2 and AA-Briefcase received improved sampling and a re-anchored Elo scale so that ratings stay stable as new models are added. For SciCode, the grading sandboxes were made more robust, so that slow but correct code counts as a pass. ## Anthropic Ahead, OpenAI Behind The upper end of the table keeps its familiar shape. Claude Fable 5.1 tops the Index, [the model that arrived recently as Anthropic’s most capable and also its pricier offering](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/fable51-anthropic/). LLMs.content: # [AI Changes Everything](/) # AI Week in Review 26.09.05 ### World Labs Atlas, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, HY4 Preview, Gemini 3.8 Flash & Flash Cyber, Muse Spark 1.3, Qwen3.8-Max 0902, Qwen-Drive-1.0, MAI-Transcribe-2, Muse Voice Transcribe, OpenClaw 2.0. [Patrick McGuinness](https://substack.com/@patmcguinness) Figure 1. World Labs Atlas can now model the world with spatial intelligence. #### Top Tools: World Labs Atlas Fei-Fei Li’s **[World Labs launched its Atlas spatial intelligence model](https://www.worldlabs.ai/blog/atlas)**, a next-generation “omni” world model designed to generate, reconstruct and simulate coherent 3D environments. Atlas can do it all when it comes to recreating physical space: It can create camera-controlled videos lasting up to one minute at 1440p, reconstruct real locations from sparse photographs, output 3D point clouds and Gaussian splats, reframe recorded action from new camera angles, generate images and 360-degree panoramas, and construct simulated environments for robotics training. Atlas is a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer trained to operate across text, images, video, camera positions and 3D depth data. Atlas grounds these inputs within a shared **spatial context** so it can maintain consistent geometry while generating new views and imagining unseen portions of a scene. Figure 2. One feature of Atlas is reconstructing 3D scenes from images, then using that reconstruction to output images from different camera viewpoints. This grounding in spatial context makes it a very flexible and powerful AI for physical rendering of all types. This is an important AI model release because it advances world models towards real-world capability as a foundational model for simulations, world-building, and image, video, and 3D asset generation. LLMs.titleZh: Can AI Now Design PCBs That Just Work?
LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#content) # Can AI Now Design PCBs That Just Work? [No comments](https://hackaday.com/2026/09/05/can-ai-now-design-pcbs-that-just-work/#respond) * by: [Maya Posch](https://hackaday.com/author/mayaposch/) [September 5, 2026](https://hackaday.com/2026/09/05/ "September 5, 2026 - 7:00 pm") ![](https://hackaday.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/openai_gpt-6_astra_kicad_showcase.jpg?w=800) With the recent release of its GPT-6 Astra model, OpenAI explicitly pushed the claim that it is capable of designing complete circuit boards in KiCad, starting from a provided schematic and outputting a fully routed PCB that theoretically could be sent off to be manufactured. This of course raises the question whether this is just a nifty party trick that works under strictly controlled conditions like most auto-routing tools, or whether there’s more to it. In a [recent [EEBench] blog post,](https://eebench.org/blog/can-ai-design-circuit-boards-yet/) OpenAI’s claims are put to the test. Back in 2024, [we looked at](https://hackaday.com/2024/06/24/testing-large-language-models-for-circuit-board-design-aid/) how LLMs handle circuit board design, starting with the schematic. The conclusion was that you might as well just do it all by hand. Tracking progress here, [[EEBench](https://eebench.org/methodology.html)] is an electrical engineering agent benchmark that tests how effective these so-called AI agents are at performing useful hardware engineering work. As their methodology already makes clear, creating a populated and routed PCB from a schematic is just one step of many. Consequently, GPT-6 Astra scores 69.3% (+/- 10%) on their benchmark, roughly in the same ballpark as Claude Opus 5, albeit cheaper and faster. It should be noted that [EEBench] is run by the developers behind [Atopile](https://github.com/atopile/atopile), which is a code-based system for creating PCBs in KiCad with a strong focus on use by such AI agents. Despite this, the blog post makes it clear that there is still a long way to go before hardware engineers can receive their pink slips and take up another profession. After all, while vibe-coding a quick prototype PCB can be a nice shortcut, for a one-off project PCB, most boards are expected to handle all the edge cases, be fully validated by multiple independent engineers, and have passed stringent testing before committing to a production run. This of course raises the question whether this is just a nifty party trick that works under strictly controlled conditions like most auto-routing tools, or whether there’s more to it. In a [recent [EEBench] blog post,](https://eebench.org/blog/can-ai-design-circuit-boards-yet/) OpenAI’s claims are put to the test. The conclusion was that you might as well just do it all by hand. Tracking progress here, [[EEBench](https://eebench.org/methodology.html)] is an electrical engineering agent benchmark that tests how effective these so-called AI agents are at performing useful hardware engineering work. As their methodology already makes clear, creating a populated and routed PCB from a schematic is just one step of many. Consequently, GPT-6 Astra scores 69.3% (+/- 10%) on their benchmark, roughly in the same ballpark as Claude Opus 5, albeit cheaper and faster. It should be noted that [EEBench] is run by the developers behind [Atopile](https://github.com/atopile/atopile), which is a code-based system for creating PCBs in KiCad with a strong focus on use by such AI agents. Despite this, the blog post makes it clear that there is still a long way to go before hardware engineers can receive their pink slips and take up another profession. After all, while vibe-coding a quick prototype PCB can be a nice shortcut, for a one-off project PCB, most boards are expected to handle all the edge cases, be fully validated by multiple independent engineers, and have passed stringent testing before committing to a production run. [Open](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=io.quasa.quasaconnect) [English](/)[Русский](/ru)[हिन्दी](/hi)[Español](/es)[Français](/fr)[简体中文](/zh)[العربية](/ar)[Português (Brasil)](/pt)[Bahasa Indonesia](/id)[বাংলা](/bn)[日本語](/ja)[Deutsch](/de)[اردو](/ur)[Türkçe](/tr)[Tiếng Việt](/vi)[한국어](/ko) [Rewards](/rewards)[For brands](/projects)[Quasa Connect](/quasa-connect) Sign inMy cabinet[Sign in](/login) [AI & Automation](/insights/topics/ai-automation) # Lasso’s Guardrail Runs on CPUs in Under 5ms—Its Benchmark Is In-House |Author: [QUASA Editorial Team](/team#editorial-team)|5 min read| 1 Lasso Security introduced LEAP on September 2, 2026, as a transformer-free guardrail for inspecting AI requests and agent actions on ordinary CPUs. The company’s [LEAP launch release](https://www.lasso.security/resources/lasso-security-announces-future-of-ai-security-with-cpu-based-guardrails) claims decisions in under five milliseconds, no GPU footprint for LEAP and thousands of times the throughput of existing guardrails. The launch coincided with $30 million in new funding, but not with independent performance validation. [SiliconANGLE’s September 2 coverage](https://siliconangle.com/2026/09/02/lasso-security-launches-cpu-only-ai-guardrail-raises-30m/) records both announcements and explicitly identifies the latency and throughput benchmarks as Lasso’s own, leaving the speed, detection quality and cost advantage unverified by third-party testing. ## LEAP is the CPU fast path, not the whole architecture LEAP is one of two engines in Lasso’s design. A tiered routing layer directs most traffic to LEAP for an inline decision, while cases requiring interpretation of policies written in plain language move to RAPID, a self-hosted large-language-model judge. This distinction narrows the claim that the system works without GPUs. LEAP is designed to run on standard processors, but GPUs do not disappear from every possible decision because difficult cases can move to RAPID. A customer’s total hardware requirement would therefore depend on the proportion of traffic resolved by LEAP, the escalation rate and the infrastructure used to host RAPID. The architecture could avoid invoking a reasoning model for every routine request. That may matter in private-cloud, regulated and air-gapped environments where inspection must remain close to applications and data, but the public materials do not quantify the routing split in a representative deployment. ## The possible saving depends on routing and detection quality The cost case is plausible because CPU-only inspection could change the unit economics of high-volume traffic. If LEAP resolves most requests while maintaining acceptable detection quality, an operator could use CPU capacity for the fast path and reserve model inference for a smaller escalation workload instead of applying a model-based judge to every event. That is a conditional advantage, not a demonstrated saving. A meaningful comparison must include request volume, CPU utilization, replica count, peak-capacity headroom, RAPID infrastructure or model costs, network transfer, observability and operational labor. Processor prices alone do not establish total deployment cost. Security outcomes can outweigh compute savings. False positives create costs when legitimate agent actions are delayed or blocked, while false negatives can expose data or permit unsafe actions. The relevant economic measure is therefore cost at a matched level of detection quality and service reliability, not latency or throughput in isolation. The financing expands the resources available to Lasso without validating those economics. The platform turns a prompt, outline, PDF, Word or Excel file, Notion page, or website URL into a 10-to-50-slide deck in under a minute, with native editable PowerPoint export and a Brand Sync feature that applies a company’s visual identity automatically, generating in more than 80 languages. The original insight is in the pricing and the growth curve together. That shift changes who inside a revenue organization actually controls what a prospect sees in the room, and it puts pressure on enablement leaders to govern brand and messaging consistency through a tool’s settings rather than through manual review. HPE stock rose more than 7% in premarket trading, according to Stocktwits, as investors digested both a strong fiscal third-quarter earnings report and a fresh reminder that Nvidia’s newest CPU architecture, not just its GPUs, is now central to HPE’s growth story. The catalyst combines two threads that had already been building for months: HPE’s September 2 earnings beat, which showed AI systems orders climbing faster than revenue, and a server platform built around Nvidia’s Vera CPU that HPE and Nvidia have been promoting since it was first shown on stage in Taipei in June. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang summed up the pitch in a line that outlets including Stocktwits have now repeated across market coverage: “Agentic AI has arrived, and it needs a new CPU.” For HPE, a company that spent much of the last decade being written off as a legacy enterprise hardware vendor, the moment amounts to a bet that agentic AI, not generative AI chatbots, is the next multi-year hardware upgrade cycle in the broader [AI chip market](/ai-chips-2026/). · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. You browse, download to Automatic1111 / ComfyUI / Forge, or generate in the browser and spend Buzz. Most posts show seed, sampler, and which LoRAs were stacked — that reproducibility is the real product. Free covers browsing, downloads, and a trickle of daily Buzz. Bronze is $10/month (10k Green Buzz, ad-free, priority queue). Silver is $25. Gold is $50. Creators can charge a per-generation fee or sell access, with caps tied to tier. civitai.com is the PG-13 front door; unrestricted galleries live on a separate domain. Quality ranges from excellent fine-tunes to noisy copies. Read the license on every file before you ship client work. 𝐂𝐎𝐑𝐄 𝐒𝐓𝐑𝐄𝐍𝐆𝐓𝐇𝐒: • Largest public LoRA / checkpoint shelf • Generation metadata on almost every image • In-browser test before you download 6 GB • Creator fees and a compensation pool • Covers SD1, SDXL, Pony, Flux, and newer stacks 𝐈𝐃𝐄𝐀𝐋 𝐅𝐎𝐑: Hobbyists and artists who want a specific style or character adapter, not people who only need one Midjourney-like box. 𝐇𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐋𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐓𝐒: • Cloud LoRA training without a home GPU • Leaderboards and collections for discovery • Civitai Link to sync resources locally • Free daily Buzz for light generate-and-browse • Prompt + seed sharing that actually teaches 𝐏𝐎𝐓𝐄𝐍𝐓𝐈𝐀𝐋 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐈𝐃𝐄𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍𝐒: • Three-color Buzz system is messy • Pages can load slowly under heavy media • Model quality is uneven — check samples • Licenses and likeness rules are on you • Membership and crypto Buzz purchases add up if you generate all day 𝐎𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐀𝐋𝐋 𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐃𝐈𝐂𝐓: 4.4/5 𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐑𝐒 Civitai is still the default library if you run local or hybrid image models. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#primary) [![Diff](https://diff.wikimedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/1024px-Wikimedia-logo.svg_-1.png?fit=1024%2C1024)](https://diff.wikimedia.org/) # Wikidata Community Summit @ COSCUP 2026 by [Hunghoro](https://diff.wikimedia.org/author/hunghoro/ "Posts by Hunghoro") [Translate this post](#translate-post) * [Wikidata MCP Server](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:MCP) * [Wikidata Embedding Project](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Embedding_Project#cite_note-1) * [Wikidata Vector Database](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Vector_Database#API_endpoints) **2026. Aug. 9th (Saturday)** Under the storm of Typhoon Dolphin, COSCUP 2026 commenced, bringing partners from around the world together to celebrate the value of open technology. The Conference for Open Source Coders, Users & Promoters (COSCUP) is one of the biggest open source events in Taiwan. This year, one topic dominated the community: Artificial Intelligence, or Agent in the concurrent stage. This year, our joint track of Wikidata and OpenStreetMap not only showcased how our respective platforms contribute to the open community, but also explored how open data and open technology can support the rapidly developing world of artificial intelligence. One highlight was our presentation with our partner from Wikimedia Deutschland, focusing on the Wikidata MCP Server and the Wikidata Embedding Project. Artificial Intelligence has come to the stage like a storm and quickly become one of the most discussed technologies across every industry. No matter which side of the fence you are on, one thing is the same: we want to know more about it and how it may affect our lives. However, much of the discussion throughout the internet is filled with empty buzzwords and misinformation from companies with various interests. The problem is not necessarily malicious intent but the fact that people, including the sources they are quoting, simply do not have enough access to the information they need to understand the technology they are discussing. Just like previous technology ‘booms’, such as cryptocurrency and NFTs, Artificial Intelligence, and now the so-called Agents, is a market phenomenon of attention crowding around something new and potentially profitable, and thus money floods in. However, unlike its predecessors, AI is ‘real’ in a sense that it has the potential to reshape, and possibly damage, many systems of trust that we humans have built through centuries of mutual understanding and respect for ourselves and others. AI Agents are not inherently disruptive or destructive; it is how we use them that is causing all the trouble. If we want the technology to become a tool for a better future, we first need to understand how the tool works. ## The Problem with LLMs A Large Language Model, or LLM, at its simplest, is an algorithm that predicts words based on the material it has been provided. Its strength comes from recognizing patterns in a given language and mimicking the ‘natural language’ according to the probability of words appearing together. But this also reveals its fundamental limitation. All it captures is the *distribution* of words appearing in languages, not necessarily the *why* and *how* behind them. It can produce an answer that looks and sounds correct without having any understanding of whether the information corresponds to reality or is actually true. Hallucinations, gibberish, and blatantly false answers are ultimately extensions of this limitation. The man in the box never understands Chinese; it just appears to. This does not mean we need the LLM to become a genie in a lamp that knows everything. The bottleneck is never the generation of more knowledge. It is discovering, retrieving, and acting upon the right information. To achieve this, there is no reason to reinvent the wheel of synthesizing the generation of natural knowledge; instead, what we need is to have the preexisting systems align properly. [![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh5UOCWTkC4W5qW8jkDjtfCM4ObQBgPLRO6CJE1FDX7b4jsx_jj0lveSBrhJB3BHvdp1Coow38hDo-UN7Srob5AMWI_AYYxYwnCc8Z22D2lAEgJisap8rHo2LjLBeqTDO-8T91q0kR12iNps0IhgXi4hIBvfQ1c4UzGuyMDI8IrWhdmW6lj-41Yw6FR-rf7/s1600-rw/brecht-corbeel-M2w18t7LX78-unsplash.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh5UOCWTkC4W5qW8jkDjtfCM4ObQBgPLRO6CJE1FDX7b4jsx_jj0lveSBrhJB3BHvdp1Coow38hDo-UN7Srob5AMWI_AYYxYwnCc8Z22D2lAEgJisap8rHo2LjLBeqTDO-8T91q0kR12iNps0IhgXi4hIBvfQ1c4UzGuyMDI8IrWhdmW6lj-41Yw6FR-rf7/s1920/brecht-corbeel-M2w18t7LX78-unsplash.jpg) Image: [Unsplash - Brecht Corbeel](https://unsplash.com/@brechtcorbeel) Before you prompt AI to answer another question or perform another task, a Wake Forest computer scientist wants you to know it could expose your sensitive data. Ying Zhang, an assistant professor in Wake Forest University’s Department of Computer Science, studies security in software engineering. Her latest research, “[How Your Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills(opens in a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03070),” explores how large language model (LLM) agents make data vulnerable to attacks. * **LLM agents** are autonomous AI systems that analyze circumstances to plan and execute multi-step actions to achieve a goal. * A **skill** is a reusable software extension that gives an LLM agent new capabilities. By installing skills into LLM agents—like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor—developers can teach agents to perform specialized tasks, such as accessing a database or analyzing domain-specific information. * The **credentials** in danger of exposure include secret identification meant to allow two systems to talk together safely, without creating access to sensitive data. The exposure happens through the use of third-party AI agent skills. The tasks the skills perform could be anything from creating a presentation using your notes to scanning financial documents for compliance issues. Open Source AI.content: * [Home](https://ximitime.com/ "Xiaomi News") * [News](https://ximitime.com/category/news/ "News") # Xiaomi TabLDM: Open-source data model tops benchmark [Emir Bardakçı](https://ximitime.com/author/trzpro/) Sep. 5, 2026, 13:08 2 mins read [0 Comments](#comments) Xiaomi has released an open-source large foundational model for structured tabular data called Xiaomi-TabLDM. The model is designed to handle both classification and regression tasks across various tabular datasets without needing task-specific retraining or tuning. It aims to simplify deployment in industries where tabular data is common, such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and logistics. ## Model Design and Pretraining Approach Xiaomi-TabLDM is pretrained solely on synthetic datasets generated by structural causal models (SCM). These datasets cover various scales, variable types, dependencies, and functional relations to broaden the model’s training distribution. The architecture includes dual-stream feature grouping for finer relational modeling, lightweight attention residuals, and a sparse mixture-of-experts mechanism to expand capacity without large computational overhead. For inference, the model employs Test-Time Scaling. This technique improves prediction accuracy by increasing computing effort during inference while keeping pretrained parameters fixed. ## Benchmark Performance and Efficiency The model ranks in the top tier across four major public benchmarks. It secured first place in regression on the OpenML-CTR23 leaderboard, and second place on TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO regression tasks. For classification, Xiaomi-TabLDM topped the TALENT binary classification task. In the TabArena regression benchmark, Xiaomi-TabLDM balanced performance and speed effectively. It achieved the second highest Elo rating while reducing training time by 82% and inference time by 68% compared to the top model TabFM. (Elo ratings here measure relative performance ranking.) ## Industrial Validation and Practical Benefits Tests in real-world industrial scenarios demonstrated Xiaomi-TabLDM’s superior accuracy and adaptability over traditional machine learning models like XGBoost. In material property prediction, the model improved prediction accuracy by 130% without any fine-tuning, cutting invalid sample tests by about 90%. For part weight predictions, it reduced error sample rates by 31%. In production component prediction, mean error dropped 54%, with a further 62% error reduction after introducing only about 30 new samples to adapt to new production conditions. ## Availability and Access Xiaomi-TabLDM is compatible with scikit-learn and can be installed via pip. Both the model’s code and pretrained weights are publicly available: * Code: [GitHub – xiaomi-tabldm](https://github.com/xiaomi-research/xiaomi-tabldm) * Weights: [Hugging Face – Xiaomi-TabLDM](https://huggingface.co/occams/Xiaomi-TabLDM) * Technical report: [arXiv 2609.03880](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03880) This release marks Xiaomi’s effort to establish a foundational model approach for structured tabular data, reducing the burden of retraining models for distinct datasets and improving prediction efficiency and accuracy across multiple domains. Users interested in trying Xiaomi-TabLDM can access the latest resources and pretrained models online. GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped [solve long-standing open problems⁠](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/) in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment.  GPT‑6 Astra is rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS. Astra is our most aligned model, with substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior—you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment. As one way that we test this, we built a new evaluation informed by the Hugging Face incident that evaluates whether a model facing a difficult or impossible task will go beyond its intended scope. Compared to GPT‑5.6 Sol, which without production safeguards went beyond the authorized target 48% of the time, GPT‑6 Astra did this in 0% of cases. ## The world’s best computer use model GPT‑6 Astra marks a new frontier in the speed, accuracy, and safety of computer use. It can take care of tedious tasks like filling out online forms, updating customer records in a CRM, and organizing your calendar. It can conduct online research and draft summaries in your email or in your document editor. It can analyze scientific data, generate plots, create a website, and run frontend QA checks to make sure all the features on that site work. It can help you autonomously install and test software, and troubleshoot problems you see on screen. These improvements are also reflected in our state-of-the-art evaluation results. These improvements also result in significant efficiency gains in real knowledge-work tasks. Combined with Astra’s efficiency, this translates to a 1.9x faster task completion compared to the current GPT‑5.6 Sol experience, on the Mind2Web benchmark. The model’s improvements on speed mean it can take on many time-consuming life tasks for you, faster than you can.[4](#citation-bottom-4) ## A step change in professional work GPT‑6 Astra pairs advances in computer use with targeted training for professional environments, to help tackle complex work tasks. The company has developed a multi-silicon cloud that distributes inference workloads across chips from six manufacturers: Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras, and d-Matrix. It recently expanded into data center infrastructure, securing multi-billion-dollar contracts. Customer count and revenue remain undisclosed, making the current valuation largely a bet on future demand. ##### Key Elements ![AI Inference 'Multi-Silicon' Startup Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million at $3 Billion Valuation](https://img.biggo.com/GqoGLyUuzs_f55cwf9xmMAeZAwDJR1k4ESg_wrbyfbE/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTA5LzQ0MGIwOTA4LTM1NDctNDFhNi04NTMyLTRlZDM1YTk4MDk4MF8xNzg4NTkxNTkwX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) AI inference infrastructure startup Gimlet Labs has raised $300 million (approximately 410 billion won) in a Series B round, securing a $3 billion valuation (approximately 4.1 trillion won). The two-year-old company has achieved unicorn status without designing its own AI chips, relying solely on software and infrastructure technology. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Arm Holdings, Microsoft's venture capital arm M12, and Samsung Ventures. Combined with the $92 million (approximately 120 billion won) raised in seed and Series A rounds, cumulative funding now totals $392 million (approximately 530 billion won). Headquartered in San Francisco, Gimlet Labs originated from a Stanford University research project and was founded in 2023. It emerged from stealth mode in October 2025, unveiling its inference platform for AI agents. CEO Zain As and the founding team previously worked together at Pixie, a Kubernetes observability company acquired by New Relic in 2020. Gimlet Labs' core offering is what it claims to be the industry's first "multi-silicon inference cloud." The technology decomposes a single AI workload into multiple stages and allocates each to the most suitable hardware—GPU, CPU, or dedicated accelerator. Developers write inference code once, and it is automatically routed to the cheapest or fastest chip available at any given time, freeing them from vendor lock-in, according to the company. The platform currently supports chips from six semiconductor manufacturers: Nvidia, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras, and d-Matrix. Gimlet Labs claims that distributing inference workloads across heterogeneous silicon can boost frontier AI workload performance by 3–10x under identical cost and power conditions, and improve throughput and interactive performance by up to 10x within the same power envelope. AI inference demands different hardware characteristics at each processing stage. The prefill stage, which processes input data all at once, is compute-intensive, while the decode stage, which generates tokens sequentially, is more sensitive to memory bandwidth. AI agents add repeated model calls and external tool usage, making workloads highly unpredictable. Gimlet Labs' strategy leverages these differences by placing each stage on the most appropriate chip, reducing the cost and power waste inherent in single-chip architectures. ### Expansion into Data Center Infrastructure Gimlet Labs has recently broadened its scope from inference software to data center infrastructure. Infra & Chips.content: × Search Pulse 2.0 # Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million Series B Led By Andreessen Horowitz At $3 Billion Valuation By Amit Chowdhry [![Pulse 2.0](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/logo-white.png)](https://pulse2.com "Pulse 2.0") Gimlet Labs Raises $300 Million Series B Led By Andreessen Horowitz At $3 Billion Valuation [![Follow Pulse 2.0 on LinkedIn](https://pulse2.com/wp-content/themes/pulse2/images/inp2.png)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/pulse2news) Gimlet Labs has raised **$300 million in Series B funding led by Andreessen Horowitz**, valuing the AI infrastructure company at **$3 billion** and bringing its total funding to **$392 million**. Sapphire Ventures participated as a major investor, while M12 and Arm joined as new investors. Existing investors Menlo Ventures and Factory also participated in the round. San Francisco-based Gimlet Labs is developing a **multi-silicon inference cloud for agentic AI**, designed to run AI workloads across multiple types of processors rather than relying on a single hardware architecture. The company’s software disaggregates AI models and assigns different phases of inference workloads to the hardware best suited for each task, with the goal of improving latency, throughput, utilization and power efficiency. Gimlet works with major AI chip companies including **NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Arm, Cerebras and d-Matrix**, allowing its infrastructure to support a combination of GPUs, CPUs and purpose-built AI accelerators. The company emerged from stealth in October 2025 with what it describes as the industry’s first multi-silicon inference software designed specifically for faster and more interactive agentic AI workloads. Gimlet’s technology is available through its own managed cloud as well as through managed deployments within customer environments. The financing follows a period of rapid commercial expansion. In March 2026, Gimlet said it had **tripled its customer base** and added one of the top three frontier AI labs and one of the top three hyperscalers as customers. Since then, the company has secured **billions of dollars in contracted revenue for Gimlet Cloud** and is scaling its managed heterogeneous infrastructure to hundreds of megawatts. Gimlet plans to use the new capital to expand operations for its multi-silicon cloud and continue growing its team. The company is positioning its architecture around the growing infrastructure demands created by agentic AI applications, which can generate enormous volumes of inference activity and require increasingly low-latency responses. Gimlet’s platform combines multi-silicon data centers, inference software and intelligent orchestration across compute nodes. Its data center architecture can integrate GPUs, CPUs and purpose-built accelerators, including SRAM-based architectures, within a unified system. Gimlet said its inference software can achieve **up to 10 times gains in throughput and interactivity** by matching different stages of AI workloads with optimized hardware architectures. The approach is also designed to improve utilization of limited computing hardware and electricity, potentially reducing the infrastructure footprint and cost required to serve large AI inference workloads. The broader market opportunity is expanding rapidly as AI spending shifts toward inference. Gimlet cited Goldman Sachs estimates that the industry could spend approximately **$765 billion on AI capital expenditures in 2026 and $7.6 trillion cumulatively from 2026 through 2031**. **KEY QUOTES:** *“AI demand is growing exponentially, while data centers and silicon can’t keep pace. The answer isn’t just more infrastructure – it’s a better architecture. Gimlet has built a new kind of inference cloud, heterogeneous by design, that matches each workload to the right silicon. By making GPUs and purpose-built accelerators work as one system, Gimlet delivers dramatically more throughput, more interactivity and more intelligence from every watt. We be...

Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # HPE Stock Surges 7% as Nvidia Vera CPU Server Debuts [2026] * [![Nadia Dubois](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/nadia-dubois/)[Nadia Dubois](https://tech-insider.org/author/nadia-dubois/ "Posts by Nadia Dubois") * [Hardware](https://tech-insider.org/category/hardware/) [Nadia Dubois](https://tech-insider.org/author/nadia-dubois/) September 5, 2026 14 min read Hewlett Packard Enterprise shares were on track to open at a fresh record high on Friday, September 4, 2026, after the company put a new Nvidia-powered server at the center of its pitch to enterprise customers racing to deploy autonomous AI agents. HPE stock rose more than 7% in premarket trading, according to Stocktwits, as investors digested both a strong fiscal third-quarter earnings report and a fresh reminder that Nvidia’s newest CPU architecture, not just its GPUs, is now central to HPE’s growth story. The catalyst combines two threads that had already been building for months: HPE’s September 2 earnings beat, which showed AI systems orders climbing faster than revenue, and a server platform built around Nvidia’s Vera CPU that HPE and Nvidia have been promoting since it was first shown on stage in Taipei in June. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang summed up the pitch in a line that outlets including Stocktwits have now repeated across market coverage: “Agentic AI has arrived, and it needs a new CPU.” For HPE, a company that spent much of the last decade being written off as a legacy enterprise hardware vendor, the moment amounts to a bet that agentic AI, not generative AI chatbots, is the next multi-year hardware upgrade cycle in the broader [AI chip market](/ai-chips-2026/). · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. Shares had already climbed sharply through the summer, touching a 52-week high near $58.79 in mid-August before pulling back ahead of the company’s fiscal Q3 2026 earnings report. HPE stock had gained roughly 159% year-to-date as of that mid-August high, with a 12-month gain of about 189%, according to a market recap covering the period. [Morgan Stanley](https://www.morganstanley.com/) had assigned the stock an Overweight rating with a $69 price target, implying analysts still saw room to run even after the run-up. The path since then has been choppier than a straight line up. HPE reported quarterly results on September 2, 2026, and the stock initially slipped, trading near $51.96 that day according to a MarketBeat earnings summary, before firming to roughly $52.83 the next session. It was two days later, on September 4, that the combination of digested earnings detail and renewed attention to the Nvidia Vera CPU server pushed HPE stock back toward record territory, with the premarket move of more than 7% reported by Stocktwits. If completed, the installation could become one of the biggest publicly known clusters built around Huawei’s Ascend processors. The project is expected to use Huawei’s next-generation Ascend 950DT accelerators to run DeepSeek’s artificial intelligence models. However, the deployment schedule could stretch beyond a year because Huawei is facing limitations in producing the chips and securing key components, according to people familiar with the matter. DeepSeek is reportedly seeking additional supplies of Huawei’s high-end processors, but production constraints could make it difficult for Huawei to meet the demand quickly. Shortages of advanced components, including high-performance memory, are expected to limit the number of Ascend 950DT processors Huawei can manufacture this year. **DeepSeek turns to domestic chips for AI inference** The planned deployment is expected to focus primarily on inference, or running AI models after they have been trained. DeepSeek is not currently expected to use the Ascend 950DT chips for model training, despite Huawei positioning the processor for demanding AI workloads. DeepSeek has previously experimented with Huawei hardware for training but has continued to rely heavily on Nvidia accelerators for this critical stage of AI development. The company has also reportedly sought greater support from Chinese authorities to secure faster access to Huawei’s chips. The planned Inner Mongolia facility forms part of DeepSeek’s broader infrastructure expansion. The company is reportedly pursuing billions of dollars in funding to build additional computing capacity. Its infrastructure plans in the region are expected to reach gigawatt scale, with the 160,000 Huawei accelerators representing only part of the facility’s overall computing resources. **China accelerates push for Nvidia alternatives** The proposed cluster comes as Beijing intensifies efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on Nvidia processors. US export restrictions have significantly limited Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia’s most advanced AI accelerators, increasing pressure on domestic manufacturers such as Huawei to close the performance gap.
